newsitem.title: JAPAN: AT&T launches cut-rate call-back service in Japan.
newsitem.headline: AT&T launches cut-rate call-back service in Japan.

text.p: AT&T Corp. launched a cut-rate international call-back service in Tokyo Wednesday, dealing a blow to the business of its Japanese partner Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co.

Analysts saw the entry by one of the world's biggest telephone operators as the start of a cut-throat price war in Japan, where, they said, KDD and two rivals created from a market liberalisation in 1989 have been in "false competition."

"Japanese firms previously avoided competition, giving time for the mini-KDDs to grow up. But now the market is not immune to a wave of international competition," said Hironobu Sawake, an analyst at the Nikko Research Centre.
Under the call-back service, users first call a switching centre in the United States and calls are then connected at cost-effective U.S. rates.

AT&T Communications Services Japan, AT&T's Japanese unit, said it would charge 240 yen ($2) for a three-minute call to Canada or the United States from Tokyo, compared with the 450 yen ($3) Japanese customers now pay.
"Today, customers rely most heavily for communications and are more actively shopping in the global marketplace," John Legere, president and CEO of AT&T Asia/Pacific, told a news conference.
"We are the first major telecommunications carrier in Japan to introduce a low-cost flat-rate international calling option," he said.
Calls to Australia, Hong Kong and Taiwan from Tokyo will cost 420 yen ($3) per three minutes, which AT&T said would be 210 yen ($1.85) to 300 yen ($2) cheaper than current rates.
The service, which will at first be offered only to business customers in Tokyo, could be used for sending data and faxes, he said.

This was the first time AT&T had started a call-back service anywhere in the world, he said. Its move comes amid opposition from KDD, which says rules must be set for international call-back services.
Japan and the United States are not entirely opposed to such a service, although 60 countries, including China and South Korea, prohibit any kind of call-back service.
"Our service is consistent with the current government guidelines," Legere said, adding that the U.S. Federal Communications Commission now considered it good for competition.

KDD and AT&T are two of the core members of World Partners, a corporate coalition aimed at providing multinational companies with hassle-free international services by linking flag carriers in each country.
"KDD can no longer cling to the good old days, when national flag carriers belonged to the same club," another analyst said. "Now even an old colleague is storming its home turf."

By the end of next year, Japan will deregulate the market for international leased phone lines. This is expected to allow more foreign operators to launch international services in Japan at relatively low costs.
